title: CPU-side bottlenecks: tokenization, request parsing, thread pools, Python overhead
content:
Summary:
We ran a focused investigation into CPU-side bottlenecks in the serving runtime. The goal was to quantify how much time is spent outside GPU inference (tokenization, request parsing, thread-pool overhead, Python GIL/context-switching) for typical text-generation workloads, and identify low-effort mitigations that reduce tail latency and CPU cost.

Background / Motivation:
- Customer reports and internal benchmarks show increasing tail latency on short prompt workloads where GPU time is small compared to end-to-end latency.
- Hypothesis: on short sequences, CPU-side preprocessing and request handling dominate p95/p99 latency.
- Key suspects: tokenizer (esp. slow vocab lookup and regex), HTTP/request parsing overhead, serialization/deserialization (JSON), thread-pool contention and context switches in Python workers, and inefficient batching logic.

Methodology:
1) Workloads:
   - S1 (short): 16-token generation from a 12-token prompt, sync request per connection (50–200 qps).
   - S2 (medium): 128-token generation, typical chat-style prompt (10–20 qps).
   - S3 (long): 1024-token generation (used as control).
2) Environment:
   - Dedicated perf hosts: c5.4xlarge-ish CPU baseline (8 vCPU), NVIDIA A10 GPU for inference.
   - Serving runtime: Python 3.11 + uvloop + Gunicorn (workers per host varied).
   - Tokenizer: HuggingFace tokenizers (Rust backend via tokenizers) for baseline, and a Python fallback slow path for edge cases.
3) Tools:
   - py-spy sampling profiler (system-wide), linux perf for kernel stacks, and custom timestamps in critical code paths.
   - Bench harness: vegeta-like generator to produce stable qps and latencies.
   - Logging/tracing: X-Request-ID propagation to attribute CPU time per request.

Key Instrumentation Points (added):
- pre_tokenize_recv_ts, post_tokenize_ts, post_request_parse_ts, enqueue_to_worker_ts, worker_start_ts, model_dispatch_ts, model_done_ts, response_serialize_ts, send_done_ts.
- Counters for queue depth and per-worker active request count.

Results (observed medians/p95s):
- S1 (short):
  - End-to-end p50/p95: 38ms / 119ms.
  - GPU kernel time median: 6ms (p95 12ms).
  - CPU pre/post overhead median: 20ms (p95 86ms).
  - Tokenization median: 6ms (p95 42ms) — significant skew from slow fallback path for non-ASCII characters and long whitespace runs.
  - Request parse + JSON deserialize + validation median: 3.5ms (p95 8ms).
  - Thread-pool enqueue->start median: 2ms (p95 18ms) — p95 correlated with queue depth and worker wakeup latency.
  - Python marshaling/serialization for response median: 1.2ms (p95 5ms).
- S2 (medium): CPU overhead reduced as GPU dominated; overall E2E p95 matched GPU p95+ small CPU tail.
- S3 (long): No CPU dominance; baseline as expected.

Detailed Findings and Root Causes:
1) Tokenization:
   - Two hot paths: fast Rust tokenizer (~sub-ms per batch) and slow Python fallback (~tens of ms) used for certain Unicode normalization cases and custom tokenization rules.
   - ~8% of requests in S1 hit fallback path due to edge-case characters (emoji, zero-width joiners) in user prompts. These accounted for ~40% of CPU tail events.
   - Tokenizer initialization per request is rare but observed in misconfigured worker pools that lazily load vocab.

2) Request parsing & JSON handling:
   - Using Python's json library via standard deserialization has median ~1–3ms; faster parsers (or C-optimized pydantic parse in strict mode) can shave ~30–50%.
   - Validation (schema checks, prompt normalization) runs on the main request thread before enqueue; complex validation functions (regex heavy) add tens of ms for malformed inputs.

3) Thread pools, worker wakeup and queuing:
   - We observed wakeup latency in Gunicorn/worker model when using gevent/eventlet vs. uvloop+async. Switching between sync and async worker types changed tail behavior.
   - High qps short-request workloads cause short-lived spikes in queue depth; workers see context-switching overhead to schedule on the CPU, amplifying tail.
   - In our setup, we used 4 worker processes each with an internal thread pool of size 8 for CPU-side processing; contention at >150 concurrent short requests caused p95 enqueue->start to jump.

4) Python overhead & GIL effects:
   - Profiling shows significant time in Python frame objects, reference counting, and garbage collections during peak. Objects created during request parsing/tokenization survive short time windows and trigger GC.
   - Using multiprocess (process-per-worker) reduced GIL contention but increased memory usage and cold-start costs.

Micro-benchmarks / Numbers:
- Tokenizer fast path: 0.2–0.8ms per request (median 0.35ms).
- Tokenizer fallback: 18–48ms (median 24ms).
- json.loads (standard lib) end-to-end: median 1.6ms, p95 6.1ms. orjson: median 0.5ms, p95 1.8ms.
- Threadpool wakeup (measured with microbenchmark): median 0.9ms, p95 9.4ms at moderate load. Under contention p95 > 25ms.

Mitigations & Experiments Run:
1) Tokenization improvements:
   - Force use of Rust tokenizers everywhere (remove Python fallback) and add pre-normalization step on ingest to canonicalize unicode. Result: S1 p95 improved from 119ms -> 78ms; tokenization p95 dropped from 42ms -> 2.6ms.
   - Cache tokenized prefixes for common prompts and system messages (LRU cache per worker). Benefit for chat-templates: p95 reduced by additional ~12ms for repeated patterns.

2) Request parsing and validation optimizations:
   - Replace standard json + custom validation with orjson + light schema checks in C (pydantic-core). Result: parse time median reduced ~60%, p95 reduced ~70%. S1 p95 improved further to ~62ms.
   - Move heavy validation to a background validation queue for non-critical checks (async). Requires schema of request to mark critical vs non-critical fields.

3) Thread pool & worker model changes:
   - Moved from process with threadpool (Python threads) to async-first model: uvicorn + uvloop + per-request CPU-bound work offloaded to a small pool of dedicated worker processes via a fast queue (shared-memory ring or unix-socket). This reduced context-switch overhead and wakeup latency.
   - Tuned worker counts to match vCPU (Nproc = vCPU / 2 for heavy GPU load); lowered thread pool sizes to avoid over-subscription.
   - Result: enqueue->start p95 reduced from 18ms -> 4.5ms under same load.

4) GC & memory behavior:
   - Disabled cyclic GC in hot paths and scoped manual GC collections after bursts reduced GC pause tail events.
   - Reduced short-lived object allocations by reusing buffers in the request pipeline (bytearray pools).

End-to-end impact (S1):
- Baseline E2E p50/p95: 38ms / 119ms.
- After tokenization + parsing + threadpool changes: 30ms / 54ms.
- Approx 54% reduction in p95 for short requests; median also improved ~20%.

Recommendations (short-term):
- Enforce Rust tokenizer usage by default and audit places that fall back to Python. Add telemetry to count fallback occurrences and the offending input patterns.
- Deploy orjson and pydantic-core for parsing/validation in the hosted runtime; keep strict mode for critical fields only.
- Adopt async-first worker model for hosted API endpoints with a small pool of pinned CPU-side helper processes for expensive CPU tasks.
- Add LRU prefix tokenization cache at worker level for common system prompts/templates. Tune cache size based on memory observations.
- Add sampling to ship full request payloads (redacted) for fallback tokenization cases.

Longer-term / Research items:
- Evaluate migrating tokenization to a lightweight C-extension integrated into the serving process to reduce cross-process overhead for VPC/Private deployments.
- Consider zero-copy JSON parsing for request->model path to eliminate extra buffer copies.
- Explore JIT/AOT of hot Python deserialization code with tools like pypy/numba for specialized validation flows.

Action items / Owners / Timeline:
- Evelyn: deploy Rust-only tokenizer flag behind a startup toggle in staging and ramp (1 week).
- Priya: migrate parsing to orjson + pydantic-core and run compatibility tests (2 weeks).
- Diego: prototype async-first worker model with helper processes and benchmark (3 weeks).
- Liam: implement tokenization prefix cache and add eviction metrics (2 weeks).
- Follow-up: rerun full p95 benchmark across regions (EU/US) after changes (end of quarter).

Appendix: useful commands / profiling notes:
- py-spy top (pid=XXX) --native --format speeds
- sudo perf record -a -g -- sleep 20; sudo perf report -g folded
- simple microbench: python micro/tokenize_bench.py --samples 10000 --use_rust
- note: when profiling, bind worker to cpu0-3 to reproduce wakeup patterns seen in production.

Open questions / Risks:
- Some enterprise customers require custom tokenization behavior (we must ensure no regressions). Solution: support opt-in custom rules via pre-tokenization hooks in a sidecar process to avoid slow fallback.
- Memory vs latency trade-offs for caching tokenized prefixes in memory-constrained Private deployments. Need per-customer tuning.

Conclusion:
CPU-side bottlenecks are the dominant source of tail latency for short requests. Many of the worst offenders are low-hanging fruit (tokenizer fallbacks, json parsing, thread wakeup). By prioritizing Rust tokenizers, faster parsing libraries, and an async-first worker model with pinned helper processes, we saw ~50%+ improvement in p95 for short workloads. Next steps are to roll the changes behind flags, collect telemetry, and validate across regional clusters and Private deployments.

Notes / History:
- 2024-09-14: initial data collection and hypothesis.
- 2024-09-20: ran tokenization-only experiment in staging.
- 2024-09-28: completed orjson migration experiment.
- 2024-10-02: compiled results and recommendations (this doc).
